title: 12 Best UX Design Staffing Agencies in 2026
summary: The 12 best UX design staffing agencies, what each actually places, and the joint-employer rule the EEOC applies when a staffing firm puts someone on your team.
body_markdown:
**Key takeaways:**


- None of the eleven staffing firms here publishes a rate. Placement pricing in this category is quoted per search, so budget comparisons have to happen on a call.
- Awesomic is first on this list but is not a staffing agency. We are a subscription, and the difference decides which one you should actually buy.
- Federal data shows temporary help employment has fallen from about 2.69 million jobs in January 2024 to roughly 2.51 million in July 2026, so the contract market is tightening rather than growing.
- A staffing placement can make you a joint employer under EEO law. The EEOC says the firm and its client can both be liable, which is worth reading before you sign.


UX design staffing agencies find you a designer to put on your team. You brief a role, they source and screen candidates, and you end up with a contractor, a contract-to-hire or a permanent employee who reports to you.


That is a genuinely different purchase from a design service, and the confusion between the two costs teams months. This list covers both, with the eleven staffing firms described as what they are and our own model labeled clearly, so you can tell which shape of problem you have before you start calling people.


Every firm below was checked on its own site in September 2026 rather than from a directory listing. Two well-known names were dropped on that check, and we say which and why in the selection section.


One audience deserves a note up front. Agencies buying design capacity to resell to their own clients have a different calculus from an in-house team, since they are managing margin rather than headcount, and we run a separate[agencies](https://www.awesomic.com/agencies) offering for exactly that reason.


## What a UX design staffing agency actually does


A staffing agency sells you access to people, not finished work. It runs sourcing and screening, presents a shortlist, and handles the paperwork if you hire. The economics follow one of three shapes.


**Contract placement** bills you an hourly rate that bundles the worker's pay and the agency's markup, and the worker usually remains the agency's employee. **Contract-to-hire** does the same with an agreed conversion point, often after 90 days. **Direct hire** charges a one-time fee, commonly a percentage of first-year salary, and the person joins your payroll immediately.


None of the eleven staffing firms on this list publishes those numbers. That is normal for the category and it is the single biggest practical difference from a subscription service, where the rate is on the page. If you want to see how the models compare before you commit, our breakdown of[subscription talent versus freelance platforms](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/subscription-talent-vs-freelance-platforms-what-business-leaders-need-to-know) sets them side by side.

### Aquent


**Overview:** A creative staffing firm that describes itself as the leading global creative staffing company, with more than 40 years behind it, placing marketing, creative and design talent on temporary, contract-to-hire and permanent terms for large organizations.


**Core services:**


- Temporary staffing for deliverables through to long-running projects
- Contract-to-hire with a 90-day assessment period before conversion
- Permanent placement across marketing, creative and design


**Industries served:** Technology, retail, financial services, healthcare, consumer brands


**Pricing:** Nothing is published. Contract work is billed at an hourly rate that includes the markup, and permanent placement is quoted per search.


**Pros:** genuine enterprise scale, a defined 90-day contract-to-hire path, deep bench across creative disciplines


**Cons:** no published pricing, better suited to larger requisitions than a single startup role, and UX is one specialism among many rather than the focus


**Notable clients or work:** Works with large marketing and design organizations, and has built a proprietary AI portfolio search tool for creative hiring.


**Why it made this list:** It is the default choice at enterprise scale, and its contract-to-hire structure is the clearest published process here.


**Final verdict:** The safest large-scale option, and overkill for a team hiring its first designer.


### Robert Half Marketing & Creative


**Overview:** The marketing and creative practice of one of the world's largest staffing companies, covering designers, content creators and marketers on contract and permanent terms.


**Core services:**


- Contract and contract-to-hire placement for creative roles
- Permanent placement supported by local market knowledge
- AI-assisted candidate matching across a very large candidate pool


**Industries served:** Effectively all sectors, from small business to global enterprise


**Pricing:** Quoted only. Fees move with the role and the metro you are hiring in.


**Pros:** more than 300 locations worldwide, 75 years of staffing experience, states it can often fill a role in as little as 48 hours


**Cons:** no published pricing, a generalist firm where UX is a sub-specialism, and service quality varies by local office


**Notable clients or work:** Serves a very broad client base across small business and enterprise; publishes annual salary guidance for creative roles.


**Its strongest suit:** Geographic reach. If you need someone on-site in a specific city, few firms can match the coverage.


**Final verdict:** A reliable generalist, best used when location matters more than deep UX specialism.


### UX Hires


**Overview:** A recruiting firm dedicated to UX and product design roles rather than to creative staffing broadly, which makes it the most precisely targeted option on this list.


**Core services:**


- Placement of product designers, UX/UI designers and AI designers
- UX researchers across both qualitative and quantitative methods
- UX writers, content designers, UX leads and front-end UX engineers


**Industries served:** SaaS companies, enterprise digital teams, startups, IT and software firms, creative agencies


**Pricing:** Not published anywhere on the site. Terms are described as flexible and settled per engagement.


**Pros:** genuinely UX-specific rather than creative-generalist, unusually granular role coverage including researchers and UX writers, positions around capability gaps rather than headcount


**Cons:** no published pricing, a smaller firm than the enterprise players, and less useful if your need spans wider marketing roles


**Notable clients or work:** Positions explicitly around product, design and technology leaders solving capability and capacity problems.


**Where it earns its fee:** Knowing the difference between a UX researcher and a product designer, which generalist recruiters routinely conflate.


**Final verdict:** The first call if the role is specifically UX and you want a recruiter who understands it.


### Onward Search


**Overview:** A staffing firm covering marketing, creative and technology talent together, positioned around helping those teams adapt to AI-driven ways of working.


**Core services:**


- Contract and freelance placement across creative and digital roles
- Permanent placement for marketing and technology teams
- Talent solutions bundled with advisory on team structure


**Industries served:** Technology, marketing, media, enterprise creative teams


**Pricing:** You get a number after submitting a talent request, not before.


**Pros:** covers creative and technology in one firm, active in AI-era skills, established presence with a broad role catalog


**Cons:** no published pricing, UX sits within a wider creative and tech remit, and the AI positioning is broad rather than specific


**Notable clients or work:** Runs an AI Portfolio Show for creative talent and publishes hiring insight for marketing and creative teams.


**Best angle:** Teams hiring across the creative and technical boundary who would rather use one firm than two.


**Final verdict:** A solid middle option, particularly when a role straddles design and engineering.


### Everforth Creative Circle


**Overview:** A creative and marketing staffing firm offering flexible arrangements from a single freelancer through to a full project team. Note the name: it now trades as Everforth Creative Circle rather than Creative Circle alone.


**Core services:**

**Notable clients or work:** Publishes an annual salary guide and a talent sentiment report drawing on a survey of more than 2,000 of its own candidates.


**Why it made this list:** The published compensation research is genuinely useful even before you engage them.


**Final verdict:** Worth a call when the scope might grow from one designer to a small team.

### Motion Recruitment


**Overview:** A technology recruitment firm with a distinct Product and UX practice sitting alongside software, data and infrastructure, so designers are hired into an engineering-literate process.

**Industries served:** Software companies, engineering-led product organizations, technology teams

**Pros:** designers are recruited by people who understand the engineering context, strong contract market presence, publishes salary trend data


**Cons:** no published pricing, UX is one practice within a tech-first firm, and pure brand or marketing design is not its strength


**Notable clients or work:** Publishes tech salary and market trend research covering more than 100 roles.


**Where it earns its fee:** Hiring a designer who has to work daily with engineers, which it understands better than a creative-only firm.


**Final verdict:** The right call when the designer will sit inside a product engineering team.


### Academy UX


**Overview:** A UX recruiting firm that treats hiring as part of building a design organization, working through assessment, recruiting strategy and implementation rather than simply filling a requisition.


**Core services:**


- Assessment of your current design structure, gaps and role definitions
- A recruiting strategy covering sourcing, engagement and interview process
- Implementation support for evaluating and retaining the people you hire


**Industries served:** Companies building or scaling an internal design function


**Pricing:** Scoped per company, with no figures shown publicly.


**Pros:** addresses role definition before sourcing, useful when you are unsure what to hire, focuses on retention as well as placement


**Cons:** no published pricing, the consultative approach is slower than a straight search, and it is more than you need for one contractor


**Notable clients or work:** Positions around building and scaling design organizations end to end.


**Best angle:** A company hiring its first design leader and unsure how the team should be shaped.


**Final verdict:** The most strategic option here, and the least suited to an urgent single contract role.


### Artisan Talent


**Overview:** A creative staffing agency placing digital, creative, marketing and AI talent, operating across a defined set of US metropolitan markets.


**Core services:**


- Freelance and contract placement for creative and digital roles
- Direct-hire placement across marketing and design
- Support for both the hiring team and the placed candidate


**Industries served:** Healthcare, consumer, agencies, in-house marketing teams


**Pricing:** Placement terms come on a call; the site lists none.


**Pros:** named coverage across twelve US metros, strong published client testimonials, responsive on small and difficult requisitions


**Cons:** no published pricing, smaller reach than the national firms, and UX is part of a broader creative offering


**Notable clients or work:** Names coverage across Atlanta, Boston, Chicago, Cincinnati, Denver, Houston, Indianapolis, Los Angeles, Miami, New York, San Francisco and Seattle.


**Why it made this list:** It is candid about being a relationship-led firm rather than a volume one, and its clients say so publicly.


**Final verdict:** A good regional option, especially for hard-to-fill single roles.


### iCreatives


**Overview:** A long-established creative staffing and recruiting agency covering marketing, design, UI and UX talent on both freelance and full-time terms.


**Core services:**


- Freelance placement for short-term creative and UX needs
- Full-time recruiting across design and marketing roles
- Coverage extending into video and gaming as well as UI and UX


**Industries served:** Agencies, in-house creative teams, gaming, marketing organizations


**Pricing:** Withheld until an initial conversation has happened.


**Pros:** more than 35 years in creative staffing, commits to responding within 25 minutes, covers freelance and permanent equally


**Cons:** no published pricing, broad creative remit rather than UX depth, and the response-time promise is conditional on when you call


**Notable clients or work:** Publishes client review scores and covers design, marketing, video, gaming and UX placement.


**Its strongest suit:** Speed of first response, which matters more than it sounds when a project is already late.


**Final verdict:** A dependable generalist with unusually fast intake.


### Mediabarn


**Overview:** A focused creative staffing agency placing creative, marketing, UX and design professionals, and one of the few firms here that publishes a street address.


**Core services:**


- Contract placement for creative, marketing and UX roles
- Contract-to-hire arrangements with a defined conversion path
- Direct-hire recruiting for design and digital teams


**Industries served:** Government-adjacent, technology and commercial teams in the DC area and nationally


**Pricing:** Absent from the site. Each placement is priced against the role.


**Pros:** deliberately narrow focus on creative and UX roles, publishes a verifiable address at 2200 Clarendon Blvd in Arlington, Virginia, positions against generalist staffing firms


**Cons:** no published pricing, a smaller bench than the national firms, and strongest in one metro despite national coverage


**Notable clients or work:** Places creative, marketing, UX and design professionals with companies in Washington, DC and nationwide.


**Where it earns its fee:** Screening specifically for the roles creative and digital teams actually fill, rather than adjacent ones.


**Final verdict:** A strong regional specialist, particularly for teams in or near Washington, DC.

## How we chose these twelve


Three checks decided the list, and two firms that rank well for this keyword did not survive them.


The firm had to **actually place design talent** . We read each candidate's own homepage and services pages in September 2026 rather than accepting a directory category, which is the check that matters most here because staffing firms pivot and directories do not follow.


**Mondo** was dropped on it: its site now leads with hiring AI engineers, machine learning specialists, prompt engineers and computer vision scientists, which is a tech search practice rather than a design one. **Razoroo** went the same way, presenting as a technical recruiting firm in Austin rather than a creative one. Directory categories are a poor guide generally, which is why our[talent marketplace cheat sheet](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/talent-marketplace-cheat-sheet-speed-cost-quality) compares the routes on speed and cost instead.


We also recorded what each firm publishes about location rather than inferring it. Only Mediabarn publishes a full street address on its contact page, and Artisan Talent names the twelve metros it covers. For the rest we say nothing about headquarters, because guessing one is the same class of error as inventing a price.


Finally, we checked pricing honestly. Not one of the eleven staffing firms publishes a rate, so their rows all read "Quoted" and we resisted the temptation to repeat markup percentages that circulate in comparison articles without a source.


## What to check before you sign with a staffing agency


The differences that matter are contractual, and most of them are invisible on a website.


- The markup on a contract rate, expressed as a percentage, not just the hourly bill rate
- The conversion fee if a contractor becomes permanent, and when it drops to zero
- The replacement guarantee period on a direct hire, and whether it is a refund or a re-search
- Who employs the worker, and therefore who carries payroll, insurance and liability
- Whether the firm has placed your specific role before, or only adjacent ones


Marketplaces answer some of these questions differently, and our[list of talent marketplaces](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/ultimate-list-talent-marketplaces-for-businesses-in-2025) sets out where each model puts the screening burden.


That fourth point carries real legal weight. The EEOC's[guidance on contingent workers](https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/guidance/enforcement-guidance-application-eeo-laws-contingent-workers-placed-temporary) states that where both the staffing firm and its client have the right to control the worker, and each has the statutory minimum number of employees, they are covered as **joint employers** , and both can be liable for a violation. Anti-discrimination obligations do not transfer to the agency simply because the agency issues the paycheck.


## How much does a UX design staffing agency cost?


Because no firm here publishes rates, the honest version of this section is a comparison of the three cost structures rather than a table of vendor prices.


Route How you pay What drives the number Ends when


Contract placement Hourly bill rate including agency markup Seniority, market, contract length You stop the assignment


Contract-to-hire Hourly rate, then a conversion fee Length of contract before conversion Conversion, often at 90 days


Direct hire One-time fee, usually a share of salary First-year salary and search difficulty The guarantee period expires


Design subscription Flat monthly fee The tier you choose You pause or cancel


Two of those four end with a salary on your payroll, which is where the real cost sits. The market context is worth knowing too. The Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks temporary help services employment in its[Current Employment Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/ces/) survey, series CES6056132001, which put the sector at about **2.51 million jobs in July 2026** , down from roughly **2.69 million in January 2024** . The contract labor pool has been shrinking for two years.


A tightening contract market tends to mean longer searches and firmer rates. That is the argument for deciding early whether you need a person or you need the work done, because the two routes are diverging in cost. Teams that start from the open marketplaces usually end up comparing[Upwork alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/10-upwork-alternatives-for-instant-talent-on-demand) before they reach an agency at all.


## Should you hire, or buy the capacity?


Hire when the work is permanent, when the designer needs deep institutional context, or when you want someone who will still be there in three years shaping the product. No subscription replaces that, and we would not claim otherwise.


Buy capacity when the queue is the problem. If design work is piling up, if a launch is blocked, or if you are covering a gap while a search runs, a subscription starts in days rather than weeks and stops when you stop needing it. Plenty of teams run both: a subscription covering the backlog while a staffing firm runs the permanent search.


There is a third answer that is often right for smaller companies. If you are not certain the role is permanent, hiring is an expensive way to find out. Founders reaching that conclusion are increasingly[leaving freelance marketplaces](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/why-founders-are-leaving-freelance-marketplaces) too, because the screening burden simply moves rather than disappearing.


## Making the call


Write down what you will hand this person in their first month. If the list is a permanent set of responsibilities, run a search and use one of the eleven firms above. If it is a queue of tasks, you want capacity and a subscription will get you there faster.


Risk allocation is the second question. A contract placement leaves employment questions with the agency, a direct hire moves them to you, and a subscription avoids them entirely. That distinction matters more for a small company than the headline rate does, and mid-market teams weighing it can see how we structure the[mid-market](https://www.awesomic.com/mid-market) version of the same decision.


Finally, get the fee structure in writing before the shortlist arrives, not after. Conversion fees and replacement guarantees are far easier to negotiate before a firm has invested in a search, and they are the terms most likely to surprise you later.


## FAQ


### What do UX design staffing agencies actually charge?


None of the eleven staffing firms in this list publishes a rate. Contract placements are billed as an hourly rate that includes the agency's markup, contract-to-hire adds a conversion fee, and direct hire is typically a one-time percentage of first-year salary. Ask for all three numbers in writing at the start, because they are quoted per search and vary widely by role and market.


### Are design staffing agencies different from graphic design staffing agencies?


In practice most firms cover both, but the screening differs. Graphic design staffing agencies are usually assessing craft and output across brand, print and marketing assets, while a UX search should test product thinking, research literacy and how someone works with engineers. Ask which specific roles a firm has filled in the last year rather than which roles it lists.


### How long does it take to fill a UX design role?


Expect weeks rather than days for a permanent hire, and days to a couple of weeks for a contractor from a firm with an active bench. Robert Half states it can often fill a role in as little as 48 hours, which is a best case rather than a norm. If your deadline is sooner than the search, cover the work another way while the search runs.


### Do I become the employer if I use a staffing agency?


Possibly both of you do. The EEOC's guidance says that where the staffing firm and its client both have the right to control the worker and each meets the statutory employee minimum, they are joint employers and both can be liable under the anti-discrimination statutes. Confirm in the contract who handles payroll, insurance and compliance, and do not assume liability sits entirely with the agency.


### Is a design subscription a real alternative to a staffing agency?


It is an alternative to the capacity problem, not to the headcount problem. A subscription gets a vetted designer working in about a day for a published monthly fee you can stop, with no placement fee or notice period. It does not give you an employee, so if you need someone permanently on your org chart with institutional knowledge, a staffing agency remains the right route.
